input.content: An array stores elements in contiguous memory locations, which allows constant-time access by index. Inserting an element in the middle of an array requires shifting every later element one position. Dynamic arrays grow by allocating a larger block and copying the old elements, so appending is amortised constant time. Choosing between arrays and linked lists depends on whether random access or frequent insertion matters more.

A stack follows last-in, first-out order and supports push and pop operations in constant time. Function calls in most programming languages are managed with a call stack that stores return addresses and local variables. Stack overflow occurs when recursion is too deep for the memory reserved for the stack. Balanced parenthesis checking is a classic application that uses a stack to match opening and closing symbols.

A binary search tree keeps every key in the left subtree smaller than the node and every key in the right subtree larger. Searching, insertion and deletion take time proportional to the height of the tree. When keys arrive in sorted order the tree degenerates into a linked list and operations become linear. Self-balancing trees such as AVL trees perform rotations after updates to keep the height logarithmic.

A heap is a complete binary tree in which every parent is ordered with respect to its children. Binary heaps are stored efficiently in arrays because the children of index i are at positions 2i+1 and 2i+2. Inserting into a heap places the new key at the end and sifts it up until the heap property holds again. Priority queues and heapsort are the two most common uses of binary heaps.

A process is a program in execution together with its address space, registers and open files. The operating system switches between processes through a context switch that saves and restores processor state. Context switches have overhead because caches and translation lookaside buffers lose useful entries. Threads within the same process share memory, which makes communication cheap but requires careful synchronisation.

CPU scheduling decides which ready process runs next on the processor. Round-robin scheduling gives each process a fixed time quantum and moves it to the back of the queue when the quantum expires. A very small quantum increases context-switch overhead, while a very large quantum makes round-robin behave like first-come, first-served. Shortest-job-first minimises average waiting time but requires knowing burst lengths in advance.

Virtual memory gives each process the illusion of a large private address space that is mapped to physical frames by page tables. When a process touches a page that is not in memory, a page fault transfers control to the operating system, which loads the page from disk. Thrashing happens when the working sets of running processes exceed physical memory and the system spends most of its time paging. Page replacement policies such as least recently used try to evict pages that will not be needed soon.

Deadlock occurs when a set of processes each hold a resource while waiting for a resource held by another process in the set. Four conditions must hold simultaneously for deadlock: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Preventing any one of these conditions prevents deadlock, for example by ordering resources so circular wait cannot form. The banker's algorithm avoids deadlock by granting requests only when the system remains in a safe state.

TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery over an unreliable network by numbering bytes and requiring acknowledgements. A connection begins with a three-way handshake in which both sides exchange initial sequence numbers. Lost segments are detected through timeouts or duplicate acknowledgements and are retransmitted. Flow control uses the receiver's advertised window so a fast sender does not overwhelm a slow receiver.

Congestion control in TCP adjusts the sending rate according to signs of network congestion. Slow start increases the congestion window exponentially until a threshold is reached or a loss is detected. After that, congestion avoidance grows the window linearly, and a loss causes the window to be reduced sharply. These mechanisms let many flows share a bottleneck link fairly without central coordination.

Routers forward packets hop by hop using forwarding tables built by routing protocols. Distance-vector protocols share estimated distances with neighbours and converge slowly when links fail, which can cause counting-to-infinity problems. Link-state protocols flood the full topology to every router, and each router computes shortest paths with Dijkstra's algorithm. Link-state routing converges faster but requires more memory and computation at each router.

IP addresses are divided into a network prefix and a host part, and subnet masks specify where the boundary lies. Classless inter-domain routing allows prefixes of any length, which reduces wasted address space. Routers choose the forwarding entry with the longest matching prefix for each destination address. Network address translation lets many private hosts share one public address by rewriting port numbers.

A relational database stores data in tables whose rows are tuples and whose columns are attributes with defined types. A primary key uniquely identifies each row, and a foreign key references the primary key of another table to enforce referential integrity. SQL queries describe what data is wanted rather than how to retrieve it, and the query optimiser chooses an execution plan. Joins combine rows from several tables that satisfy a condition on shared attributes.

Normalisation organises tables to reduce redundancy and update anomalies. A table is in first normal form when every attribute holds atomic values, and in second normal form when no non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite key. Third normal form additionally removes transitive dependencies between non-key attributes. Denormalisation is sometimes applied deliberately to speed up read-heavy workloads at the cost of redundancy.

A transaction is a sequence of operations that the database treats as a single logical unit. The ACID properties require atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability for every transaction. Write-ahead logging records changes before they are applied so that committed work can be recovered after a crash. Aborted transactions are rolled back using the undo information stored in the log.

Concurrency control lets many transactions run at once while preserving correctness. Two-phase locking requires a transaction to acquire all its locks before releasing any, which guarantees serialisable schedules. Strict two-phase locking holds exclusive locks until commit to avoid cascading aborts. Multiversion concurrency control instead keeps older versions of data so readers never block writers.

A graph consists of vertices connected by edges, which may be directed or undirected and weighted or unweighted. Graphs can be represented with an adjacency matrix, which uses quadratic space, or an adjacency list, which uses space proportional to the number of edges. Breadth-first search explores vertices in order of distance and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. Depth-first search explores as far as possible along each branch and is used for topological sorting and cycle detection.

Dijkstra's algorithm computes shortest paths from a source in graphs with non-negative edge weights. It repeatedly selects the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance and relaxes its outgoing edges. With a binary heap the algorithm runs in time proportional to the number of edges times the logarithm of the number of vertices. Negative edge weights break its greedy assumption, so the Bellman-Ford algorithm is used instead.

A file system organises persistent data into files and directories on a storage device. Each file has metadata such as its size, owner, permissions and the locations of its data blocks, often stored in an inode. Directories map human-readable names to inode numbers, forming a hierarchical namespace. Journaling file systems record pending metadata updates so the file system can be repaired quickly after a crash.

Input and output devices are slower than the processor, so operating systems use buffering and caching to hide latency. Interrupts let a device notify the processor when an operation completes instead of the processor polling repeatedly. Direct memory access allows devices to transfer blocks of data to memory without involving the processor for every byte. Device drivers present a uniform interface to the rest of the kernel while handling hardware-specific details.

Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key to encrypt and decrypt, which is fast but requires the key to be shared securely. Public-key cryptography uses a key pair in which the public key encrypts and only the private key decrypts. In practice, protocols use public-key methods to agree on a symmetric session key and then encrypt bulk data symmetrically. Digital signatures use the private key to sign data so that anyone with the public key can verify its origin.

Transport Layer Security protects web traffic by authenticating the server and encrypting the connection. During the handshake the server presents a certificate signed by a certificate authority that the client trusts. The client verifies the certificate chain and the domain name before deriving session keys. Without certificate validation an attacker could perform a man-in-the-middle attack and read or modify the traffic.

An index is an auxiliary data structure that speeds up lookups on one or more columns. B-plus trees are the most common index structure because they keep data sorted and remain balanced with high fan-out. Range queries benefit from B-plus trees since leaf nodes are linked in key order. Every index speeds up some reads but slows down inserts and updates, because the index must be maintained.

Hash indexes map keys to buckets with a hash function and support very fast equality lookups. They cannot answer range queries efficiently because hashing destroys key order. Collisions are handled by chaining entries within a bucket or by probing for another slot. Query optimisers estimate the cost of using each available index and may choose a full table scan when an index would not help.
